blocks.html: reverse
Suppose you want to store the marks of 60 students. Writing 60 variables (m1 , m2 , …
m60 ) is impossible to manage. An array stores many values of the same type under one
name, in continuous memory locations, each reached by an index.
Real-life example: a row of lockers in a school. All lockers have the same size, they are numbered 0, 1, 2, … and you open one by its number.
Declaration: data_type name[size];

items.html: Each int uses 4 bytes, so the array uses 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.
C++ does not check the index. marks[5] or marks[-1] is a serious error (it reads or writes unknown memory).
The size of a normal array is fixed when it is created.

(a) Linear search — checks each element one by one from the start. Works on any array (sorted or not).

blocks.html: (b) Binary search — works only on a sorted array. Compare the key with the middle element; if smaller, search the left half; if larger, search the right half. Each step halves the search area.
Each step compares the key with the middle element and throws away the half that cannot contain it, so 10 elements need only 3 comparisons here.

rows: Works on unsorted and sorted arrays
Halves the search area each step

blocks.html: In bubble sort, neighbouring elements are compared and swapped if they are in the wrong order. After each pass, the largest remaining element "bubbles up" to its correct place at the end.
The sorted part grows from the right by one element each pass, so an array of n elements needs at most n − 1 passes.
To sort in descending order, change arr[j] > arr[j + 1] to arr[j] < arr[j + 1] .

blocks.html: A normal array has a fixed size. A vector (from <vector> ) is an array that can grow and shrink while the program runs. It is the closest C++ match to a Python list.

vector<int> v;                  // empty vector of int
vector<int> marks = {78, 92};   // with values
vector<string> names(3);        // 3 empty strings

blocks.html: 1. What is an array? Write its declaration syntax.
Answer: An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in continuous memory under one name, accessed by index. Syntax: data_type name[size]; e.g. int marks[60];
2. Differentiate between an array and a vector.
Answer: An array has a fixed size set at creation; a vector can grow or shrink at run time and has functions like push_back() , size() , insert() and erase() .
3. Write the output:
Answer: 8 (a[0] + a[2] + a[4] = 3 + 1 + 4).
4. How do you find the number of elements in an array?
Answer: int n = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]); — total bytes divided by the bytes of one element. For int t[] = {10, 20, 30, 40}; n = 16 / 4 = 4.
5. Write the output:
Answer: 246 — the original array is changed because arrays are passed by reference.
6. Differentiate between linear and binary search (two points).
Answer: Linear search works on unsorted data and checks every element (up to n comparisons). Binary search needs sorted data and halves the range each step (about log₂n comparisons).
7. Write a code segment to find the sum of the diagonal elements of a 3 × 3 matrix.
8. What happens if you access a[10] in an array of size 10?
Answer: Valid indices are 0 to 9. a[10] is outside the array. C++ does not check this, so it reads or overwrites unknown memory, which can give garbage values or crash the program.
